title: Given two arrays `nums1` (a subset of `nums2`), for each element in `nums1` find the next greater element to its right in `nums2`. If none exists, return -1 for that element.
shortTitle: Next Greater Element I — decreasing monotonic stack + HashMap

s1_definition.profdef: Next Greater Element uses a decreasing monotonic stack to find, for each value, the first larger value appearing to its right in linear time. You scan the larger array once, and whenever the current value is greater than the value on top of the stack, that current value is the "next greater" for the popped element, which you record in a HashMap for constant-time lookup by the query array.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya is reviewing a sequence of daily closing stock prices and wants, for each day, the next day in the future whose price is higher. She keeps a pile of "waiting" days whose answer she has not found yet. When a new, higher price arrives, it answers every waiting day on top of the pile that is lower than it, so she pops them and writes down that this new day is their next-higher day. Days still waiting at the end never find a higher day and get marked "none."
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a decreasing stack of pending values, and each new value resolves every smaller value on top of the stack as its next greater element.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Next Greater Element uses a decreasing monotonic stack to find, for each value, the first larger value appearing to its right in linear time. You scan the larger array once, and whenever the current value is greater than the value on top of the stack, that current value is the "next greater" for the popped element, which you record in a HashMap for constant-time lookup by the query array.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya is reviewing a sequence of daily closing stock prices and wants, for each day, the next day in the future whose price is higher. She keeps a pile of "waiting" days whose answer she has not found yet. When a new, higher price arrives, it answers every waiting day on top of the pile that is lower than it, so she pops them and writes down that this new day is their next-higher day. Days still waiting at the end never find a higher day and get marked "none."

**One line to remember:** Keep a decreasing stack of pending values, and each new value resolves every smaller value on top of the stack as its next greater element.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive solution checks every element against everything to its right, which is quadratic. The monotonic stack reduces this to linear by ensuring each element is pushed and popped at most once.

You scan the main array left to right. You maintain a stack that stays decreasing from bottom to top; it holds values that are still waiting for their next greater element. When the current value is greater than the stack top, the current value is the answer for that top element, so you pop it and record the mapping. For example: `while (!stack.isEmpty() && current > stack.peek()) { map.put(stack.pop(), current); }`.

After resolving everything the current value is greater than, you push the current value, because it is now itself waiting for its own next greater element. For example: `stack.push(current);`.

At the end, whatever remains on the stack has no greater element to the right, so those map to -1. For example: `while (!stack.isEmpty()) map.put(stack.pop(), -1);`. Because the query array `nums1` is a subset of `nums2`, you then simply read each answer from the map. For example: `result[i] = map.getOrDefault(nums1[i], -1);`.

The time complexity is linear because every element enters and leaves the stack exactly once, and the HashMap lookups are constant time on average. A senior nuance is why the stack stays monotonic: when a larger value arrives, it resolves and removes all smaller pending values below it in one sweep, so no element ever needs to be revisited. This "each element touched twice" property is the signature of monotonic stack problems.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India's trading desk, Priya tracks a watchlist of a few stocks and wants, for each one, the next trading day in the full price series whose price first exceeds today's price. This tells her how soon a breakout happened. Scanning the full series separately for each watched stock is wasteful. This is exactly how Next Greater Element works — one pass over the full series builds every answer.

Problem 2 — The watchlist is a subset of all tracked stocks, and lookups must be instant. This is exactly why we store each stock's next-greater price in a HashMap and then read the watchlist answers in constant time.

The mini-project builds a `NextGreaterPriceFinder` that computes the next greater value using a monotonic stack and a map, a `WatchlistService` that answers queries for a subset of stocks with logging, and a runnable demo over a price series.

sections.s5_journey:
The input series is 2450, 2400, 2500, 2460, 2600 and the watchlist is 2400, 2500, 2600.

Step 1: Read 2450. The stack is empty, so nothing is resolved. Push 2450. The stack is 2450.

Step 2: Read 2400. 2400 is not greater than 2450, so nothing resolves. Push 2400. The stack from bottom to top is 2450, 2400, which is decreasing.

Step 3: Read 2500. 2500 is greater than the top 2400, so pop 2400 and record its next greater as 2500. 2500 is also greater than the new top 2450, so pop 2450 and record its next greater as 2500. The stack is now empty. Push 2500.

Step 4: Read 2460. 2460 is not greater than 2500, so nothing resolves. Push 2460. The stack is 2500, 2460.

Step 5: Read 2600. 2600 is greater than 2460, so pop 2460 and record its next greater as 2600. 2600 is greater than 2500, so pop 2500 and record its next greater as 2600. The stack is empty. Push 2600.

Step 6: The series ends. 2600 remains on the stack with no greater element to its right, so record its next greater as -1.

Step 7: Read the watchlist from the map: 2400 maps to 2500, 2500 maps to 2600, 2600 maps to -1.

```text
2026-10-26T16:50:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Watchlist Breakout Finder
2026-10-26T16:50:00Z [INFO] Watchlist [2400, 2500, 2600] next-greater prices = [2500, 2600, -1]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Next Greater Element is the canonical monotonic stack problem, and the whole point is turning a naive quadratic scan into a single linear pass. The brute force compares each element with everything to its right, but a decreasing monotonic stack lets me resolve answers as I go. I scan the full array once and keep a stack of values that are still waiting for their next greater element, maintained so it decreases from bottom to top.

The mechanism is that whenever the current value is greater than the value on top of the stack, the current value is precisely the next greater element for that top element, so I pop it and record the mapping, repeating until the top is no longer smaller. Then I push the current value, because it now becomes a pending element waiting for its own answer. Anything still on the stack at the end never found a greater value, so those map to negative one.

I store the answers in a HashMap keyed by value, which matters because the query array is a subset of the full array. Once the map is built, every query is a constant-time lookup. The complexity is linear overall, and the reason is the signature property of monotonic stacks: each element is pushed once and popped at most once, so no element is ever revisited.

In my project at National Bank of India's trading desk, I used this to answer, for each stock on a trader's watchlist, the next trading day whose price first exceeded the current day's price, which signals how quickly a breakout occurred. One pass over the full price series built the complete answer map, and because the watchlist is only a handful of stocks, reading their breakout prices from the map was instant.
